article_sentences: Deep depression intensifies into cyclonic storm 'Murasu' over the southwest and adjoining west-central Bay of Bengal.
A scene at Marina Beach on November 1, 2026.
A deep depression over the Bay of Bengal on Sunday (November 1, 2026) intensified into a cyclone named “Murasu”.

According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), the latest storm is set to make landfall on the morning of November 3 between Nellore and Narsapur in Andhra Pradesh, with wind speeds of 100-110 kmph, gusting to 120 kmph.
Chennai and Tiruvallur District Collectors have announced that schools and colleges of the districts will be closed on Monday (November 2, 2026) due a heavy rains.
An orange alert was announced in six Telangana districts and a yellow alert in five districts in Telangana for Monday.
The cyclonic storm over Southwest and adjoining Westcentral Bay of Bengal moved west-northwestwards at a speed of 25 kmph during the past six hours.

It lay centred about 350 km east of Chennai, 400 km east-southeast of Nellore, 430 km southeast of Machilipatnam, 420 km east-southeast of Kavali, 450 km southeast of Ongole, and 520 km south of Visakhapatnam, according to IMD.

stories.headline: FPIs turn net buyers as AI trade worries trigger allocation shift
stories.title: FPIs turn net buyers as AI trade worries trigger allocation shift
stories.summary: Mumbai: After aggressively selling in September and the first half of October, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have turned net buyers of Indian equities, investing nearly $1.2 billion over the past 10 trading sessions. Concerns over the outlook for the AI trade could have prompted some overseas investors to shift allocations to beaten-down Indian equities, which have lagged behind various regional peers recently in the absence of a dominant AI industry. The recent purchases, however, may be positional flows looking for avenues that are less impacted by the AI sell-off rather than a fresh bullish call on India by global investors."Indian large-cap stocks, particularly banks and IT companies, are being viewed as an anti-AI trade, attracting model-driven flows rather than a broad-based return of long-only foreign investors, said Ritesh Jain, founder of Pinetree Macro.135441127Between October 16 and October 30, FPIs made net purchases of nearly $1.2 billion in the secondary market, according to NSDL data. On October 30, they bought equities worth ₹3,600 crore, according to provisional NSE data. In the primary market, they were buyers worth $600 million, with Jio Telecom's ₹30,188 crore IPO expected to have cornered a large chunk of these flows."There is a shift in global investment flows because of signs of a deflation in the artificial intelligence (AI) trade," said Jain. "When the AI trade is doing well, money moves from the rest of the world into the US as investors buy dollars to invest in US AI stocks. When they sell these stocks, they also move out of the US dollar."Read more: Nifty IT’s 18% rally may mark a durable leadership cycle; 35,000 next: LKP's Vatsal BhuvaIndian markets delivered a mixed performance in October. The Sensex and Nifty gained 1.9% and 2.7%, respectively, while the BSE Midcap 150 and BSE SmallCap 250 fell 4% and 6.3%. The Nifty IT index surged 17%.Overseas markets, meanwhile, saw sharp corrections, with the Nasdaq and Japan's Nikkei falling 5% each, Hong Kong's Hang Seng declining 5.5%, Shenzhen dropping 13.7%, and Taiwan and South Korea's Kospi falling 8% and 14%, respectively.Fund managers are seeing selective opportunities in India after the recent underperformance, said strategists. "A small portion of the inflows reflected selective foreign investors returning to India on a bottom-up basis, attracted by improving growth prospects and opportunities in certain technology sectors," said Gautam Chhaochharia, head of global markets, India, at UBS.Read more: Bonus issues, stock splits, dividends: Infosys, Asian Paints among over 40 stocks turning ex-date this weekThe recent buying follows a prolonged period of foreign outflows. Between January 1 and October 15, they sold equities worth over $32.7 billion amid the US-Iran war, rising crude oil prices, hardening bond yields, currency depreciation, earnings uncertainty and inflation. They had also sold equities worth over $18.8 billion in 2025.Though overseas investors bought nearly $6.15 billion in Indian equities between mid-June and August, they pulled out $8.6 billion in September and the first half of October as a spike in global oil prices and hardening of US bond yields heightened risk-off sentiment."The recent pressure on Indian markets had been driven more by global factors, including the strength of the AI trade and higher energy prices, than by domestic fundamentals," said Ben Powell, chief investment strategist for Middle East and Asia-Pacific at BlackRock Investment Institute.BlackRock remains strategically overweight on India and is closely monitoring the recent pace of foreign inflows. "We continue to closely watch the encouraging recent pace of inflows and remain strategically overweight India," he said.

stories.headline: J&K Draft Mountain Policy proposes visitor limits at tourist hotspots to check overcrowding
stories.title: J&K Draft Mountain Policy proposes visitor limits at tourist hotspots to check overcrowding
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 1: A draft policy on sustainable mountain development has proposed a major overhaul of tourism management, infrastructure development and environmental protection in Jammu and Kashmir, including daily visitor limits at popular destinations, restrictions on private vehicles, a green cess of up to Rs 2,000 for foreign tourists and tighter controls on construction in ecologically sensitive areas. The Draft Jammu and Kashmir Sustainable Mountain Development Policy (JK-SMDP 2026), dated October 12, 2026, envisages a framework to regulate tourism, protect fragile mountain ecosystems and ensure that local communities benefit from economic activity in the region. The document, which is still a draft for consideration, does not represent an approved government decision. Its recommendations would require formal approval and, where necessary, legal backing before they could be implemented. One of its key proposals is to introduce carrying-capacity limits at 15 high-pressure tourist destinations, including Gulmarg, Pahalgam, Sonamarg, Doodhpathri, Yusmarg, Gurez, Bangus, Sinthan Top, Patnitop, Katra, Paddar, Basoli and Bhaderwah. The draft proposes that scientific carrying-capacity studies be completed within 12 months. Pending these studies, interim daily visitor limits could be introduced within 100 days of the proposed policy’s approval, based on the capacity of roads, parking facilities and sanitation infrastructure. It also envisages an online registration and time-slot booking system for visitors at high-pressure destinations, supported by digital entry passes, cess collection, weather alerts and visitor data management. In a significant proposed change to tourist transportation, the draft recommends that private cars, taxis and buses be stopped at designated green gateways located approximately 10 kilometres below fragile destinations. Beyond these gateways, movement would be restricted to electric or CNG vehicles, walking, ponies or cycles. The document proposes that electric vehicle fleets be operated by local youth cooperatives, self-help groups and registered local operators, while outside operators would not be licensed. Tangmarg has been identified as a possible green gateway for Gulmarg, Pahalgam town for Aru, Betaab Valley and Chandanwari, and Sonamarg market for the Thajiwas area. Emergency, defence, disaster-response and essential local-service vehicles would be exempted. The draft also proposes a Mountain Green Cess, with different rates for domestic and foreign visitors. According to its detailed tariff table, domestic tourists would be charged Rs 500 at Zone B destinations, including Gulmarg, Pahalgam, Patnitop, Sonamarg and Doodhpathri, and Rs 1,000 at Zone A sites such as glaciers, high-altitude lakes, alpine meadows and high-altitude trekking routes. For foreign nationals, the proposed cess is Rs 2,000 at both categories of destinations. Children below 12 years, specially abled individuals and residents of the local body where a destination is situated have been proposed for exemption. Other Jammu and Kashmir residents and students on institutional tours would be charged Rs 100. The policy estimates that the cess could generate approximately Rs 750 crore annually, based on an estimated 1.5 crore to 2.5 crore tourists and a conservative average collection of Rs 500 per visitor. It proposes that the revenue be ring-fenced for destination-level environmental management, with 40 per cent allocated to waste collection, toilets and sanitation, 20 per cent to ecological restoration, 20 per cent to local employment, 10 per cent to visitor safety and rescue systems, and the remaining 10 per cent to monitoring and administration. The draft states: “Cess collected at a destination is spent at that destination; it cannot be diverted.” The document also proposes restrictions on new construction in high-risk and ecologically sensitive areas, including glacier forelands, stream corridors and identified hazard-prone zones. It calls for stronger land-use planning and environmental safeguards to prevent unregulated construction in mountain regions. On waste management, the draft envisages that every notified destination should be free of visible garbage and untreated sewage within three years. It proposes a ban on single-use plastics in notified destinations, deposit-refund mechanisms, material recovery facilities and a carry-in, carry-out system for visitors. Legacy waste at identified locations would be targeted for clearance within two years, while penalties would be introduced for violations. Disaster preparedness forms another major component of the proposed policy. It recommends multi-hazard risk mapping for hill towns, tourist destinations, pilgrimage routes and highways within three years, covering landslides, flash floods, avalanches, glacial lake outburst floods and earthquakes. It also proposes early-warning systems, trained community volunteers, rescue equipment and evacuation plans. The draft envisages automatic closure of tourist sites and routes during red alerts issued for extreme weather and other hazards. “We cannot stop cloudbursts, but we can stop them from becoming mass tragedies. The goal is zero avoidable deaths from mountain hazards,” the document states. Pilgrimage management has also been addressed, with the draft proposing science-based daily limits for yatras and religious destinations, including the Amarnath Yatra, Shri Mata Vaishno Devi, Machail Mata, Shiv Khori and Buddha Amarnath. It recommends temporary suspension of movement when weather and early-warning systems issue red alerts for cloudbursts, landslides or flash floods. The policy places considerable emphasis on creating employment opportunities for residents of mountain areas. It proposes local jobs in electric vehicle operations, waste management, recycling, guiding services, homestays, slope restoration and visitor assistance. “Protecting the mountains must put money in the pockets of mountain people. Regulation without livelihoods will fail; this Policy ties every rule to local jobs,” it states. For institutional implementation, the draft proposes a Jammu and Kashmir Mountain Development Authority and a non-lapsable J&K Mountain Green Fund. The proposed fund would receive money from the green cess, trekking and expedition fees, penalties, deposits and other sources, including government schemes, corporate social responsibility contributions and climate finance. The document also proposes that a J&K Sustainable Mountain Development Act be brought into law within one year, providing legal backing for inspections, penalties, restoration orders and enforcement measures. “A policy without legal teeth becomes a document on a shelf,” the draft states, adding that “This Policy shall move to law within one year.” The proposed implementation roadmap envisages action during the first 100 days following Cabinet approval, including the identification of three model destinations, interim visitor caps, pilot green gateways, cess collection and the launch of the proposed Mountain Pass platform. The draft identifies Gulmarg, Patnitop and Bhaderwah as possible model destinations. It also proposes a freeze on new building permissions in glacier forelands, stream corridors and identified red zones during the initial implementation phase. Over the following three years, the document envisages expansion of visitor caps, green gateways and cess collection to notified destinations, alongside risk mapping, early-warning systems and hill-town master plans. By the fifth year, it aims for notified destinations to be free of visible garbage and untreated sewage, with fossil-fuel vehicles eliminated beyond green gateways and measurable improvements in mountain ecosystems. The draft sets out a broader vision of moving Jammu and Kashmir away from mass tourism towards managed, high-value tourism, stating: “J&K will move from mass tourism to managed, high-value tourism: fewer vehicles, cleaner sites, better experiences and more income for local and specially abled people.” However, the document contains a discrepancy in the proposed cess rates. Its overview section refers to a green cess of Rs 100 to Rs 300 per visitor per site, while the detailed tariff table proposes charges ranging from Rs 100 to Rs 2,000, depending on the category of visitor and destination. The difference would need clarification before the proposal is finalised. The recommendations, if approved and backed by the required legal and administrative measures, could significantly change how tourism, construction, transportation and environmental protection are managed in Jammu and Kashmir’s mountain regions.

stories.headline: One Health, One System
stories.title: One Health, One System
stories.summary: Many outbreaks that reach a hospital begin elsewhere, in wildlife or livestock, and cross into people through food, water or close contact. By the time the first case is diagnosed, the ecological event behind the outbreak may already be weeks old. That gap between the ecological event and the clinical diagnosis is the one that One Health, marked every year on November 3rd, is meant to close. The case for One Health rests on numbers that rarely change. The CDC and the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) estimate that about six in ten known human infectious diseases can spread between animals and humans, and roughly three in four new or emerging ones originate in animals. India is exposed by its own success. It is the world's largest milk producer and has one of the largest livestock populations, and its farms, forest fringes and informal markets bring people, animals and wildlife into constant contact. In such a landscape, the first sign of a human epidemic is often a pattern in animals that nobody connected: clustered abortions in cattle, unexplained deaths in a flock, a rise in fever cases at a primary health centre. Environmental change is steadily widening that exposure. Warmer, wetter conditions lengthen the breeding season and extend the range of insect vectors. Lumpy skin disease, caused by a capripoxvirus and spread by biting flies, mosquitoes and ticks, swept through Indian cattle in 2022 and has since reached many States, including Jammu and Kashmir. It does not infect people, yet it is a public health concern: it deprives households of milk, draught power and income, and these are the families least able to absorb the loss. Climate stress works through the food chain as well. Experimental work on elevated carbon dioxide has found lower nutrient composition in crops such as wheat and rice, while droughts and floods degrade fodder. Undernourished animals can be less productive and more susceptible to disease. More pests and fungi mean heavier pesticide use, and residues drain into rivers and aquatic food webs, returning the problem to human diets. Some risks reach us quietly, through the milk pail. Raw milk can carry bacteria such as Mycobacterium bovis, Brucella and Salmonella, which cause tuberculosis, brucellosis and salmonellosis in people. Brucellosis, for example, causes undulant fever, joint pain and fatigue, symptoms easily mistaken for typhoid or tuberculosis, so the disease is under-diagnosed and under-reported. Farmers and veterinarians carry occupational risk, and consumers carry the rest. Vaccinating female calves under the National Animal Disease Control Programme protects the herd, but it does not protect a household that receives unboiled milk from the unorganized sector. Pasteurization and the cold chain are therefore public health measures as much as dairy-economy ones. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is perhaps the clearest proof that the three domains are one. The Global Research on Antimicrobial Resistance study in The Lancet estimated 1.14 million deaths directly attributable to bacterial AMR in 2021 and projected nearly 39 million cumulative attributable deaths between 2025 and 2050. Antibiotics given to animals for growth promotion, prophylaxis or unsupervised treatment select for resistant bacteria and resistance genes. These pass through manure, water, soil and food to people, and then back to animals. India banned colistin, a last-resort antibiotic, in food-producing animals in 2019, and the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has set residue limits. Enforcement, farm-level sales data and veterinary stewardship remain the weak links. The obstacle is institutional rather than scientific. Human disease surveillance sits with health authorities, animal disease reporting with animal husbandry departments, and wildlife and habitat data with forest and environment bodies. They rarely share a threshold for action, a database or a chain of command. Four global agencies, WHO, the Food and Agriculture Organization, WOAH and the UN Environment Programme, have drawn up a One Health Joint Plan of Action, but the real test is delivery in India’s districts. That begins with health, veterinary and environment teams meeting within hours of a suspected outbreak, guided by warning signs agreed in advance. It requires funded veterinary diagnostic laboratories linked to block-level dispensaries, with veterinarians treated as part of public health surveillance and not as a separate service. It requires a safer milk chain through pasteurisation and testing, antibiotics for animals sold only on prescription with sales recorded, and climate-linked surveillance of vectors and wildlife for early warning of outbreaks. Households can contribute too: boiling milk, cooking meat thoroughly, and washing produce are among the cheapest protections available. But the risk begins earlier, on the farm and in the environment. Protecting animals and the environment is part of protecting people. (The Author is a Veterinarian and an Independent Researcher. Email: dr.akhterrasool@rediffmail.com)

Antibiotics given to animals for growth promotion, prophylaxis or unsupervised treatment select for resistant bacteria and resistance genes.
These pass through manure, water, soil and food to people, and then back to animals.
India banned colistin, a last-resort antibiotic, in food-producing animals in 2019, and the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has set residue limits.
Enforcement, farm-level sales data and veterinary stewardship remain the weak links.
The obstacle is institutional rather than scientific.
Human disease surveillance sits with health authorities, animal disease reporting with animal husbandry departments, and wildlife and habitat data with forest and environment bodies.
They rarely share a threshold for action, a database or a chain of command.

Four global agencies, WHO, the Food and Agriculture Organization, WOAH and the UN Environment Programme, have drawn up a One Health Joint Plan of Action, but the real test is delivery in India’s districts.
That begins with health, veterinary and environment teams meeting within hours of a suspected outbreak, guided by warning signs agreed in advance.
It requires funded veterinary diagnostic laboratories linked to block-level dispensaries, with veterinarians treated as part of public health surveillance and not as a separate service.

It requires a safer milk chain through pasteurisation and testing, antibiotics for animals sold only on prescription with sales recorded, and climate-linked surveillance of vectors and wildlife for early warning of outbreaks.
Households can contribute too: boiling milk, cooking meat thoroughly, and washing produce are among the cheapest protections available.
But the risk begins earlier, on the farm and in the environment.
Protecting animals and the environment is part of protecting people.
(The Author is a Veterinarian and an Independent Researcher.
Email: dr.akhterrasool@rediffmail.com).

Four global agencies, WHO, the Food and Agriculture Organization, WOAH and the UN Environment Programme, have drawn up a One Health Joint Plan of Action, but the real test is delivery in India’s districts.
Lumpy skin disease, caused by a capripoxvirus and spread by biting flies, mosquitoes and ticks, swept through Indian cattle in 2022 and has since reached many States, including Jammu and Kashmir.
By the time the first case is diagnosed, the ecological event behind the outbreak may already be weeks old.

stories.headline: Jhelum is calling
stories.title: Jhelum is calling
stories.summary: River Jhelum, which is considered to be the lifeline of Kashmir, has been facing extreme ecological threat due to unabated pollution, illegal mining and encroachments. Jhelum serves a dual purpose for Kashmir—its major source for drinking water and irrigation and importantly saves the Valley from floods. Ironically the river has been fast losing both these functions in absence of conservation measures. Jhelum originates from Verinag in south Kashmir, spans over 175 sq Kms and settles in Wular lake before flowing to Pakistan Occupied Kashmir (PoK) from Baramulla district in north Kashmir. The river is propelled by four streams—Sundran, Brang, Arapath and Lidder is Anantnag district. Besides small streams like Veshav and Rambiara also fed the river with fresh lease of waters. All water bodies flow into Jhelum making it an important part of Kashmir’s interconnected hydrological system. Despite its immense ecological importance, Jhelum is facing extreme pollution as all drains from south to north Kashmir directly flow into the river. The irony is that instead of constructing Sewage Treatment Plants, authorities have set up hundreds of pumping stations to empty drains into the river. The problem is compounded by dumping of solid waste and illegal sand mining. All these factors have severely affected flora and fauna and the hydrological system of the river. Jhelum has lost its carrying capacity also. It has been observed that the river swells and overflows after incessant rains for even 2-3 days. Wetlands like Hokersar, Bemina, Narakara, Batamaloo numbal, Rakh-e-arth, Anchar and Gilsar on the left and right of Jhelum, which acted as reservoirs of floodwaters, have been encroached upon, filled and converted into colonies. Deterioration of these wetlands have affected their capacity to absorb flood water—putting extra pressure on Jhelum. Jhelum Action Plan formulated for four towns of Anantnag, Srinagar, Sopore and Baramulla to intercept, divert, transmit sewage of these areas and treat it in STPs is still on paper. The intervention of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir to restore the glory of Jhelum is timely. A division bench comprising Chief Justice Dr Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Yash Paul Bourney recently sought the report after Advocate Nadeem Qadiri, assisting as amicus curiae in the Public Interest Litigation (PIL) by Environmental Policy Group on conservation of Jhelum, raised concern over deteriorating condition of Jhelum. The Court has sought a report attesting to mining activities, proposed setting up of Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) in river Jehlum as also construction or removal of embankments for flood control of the waterbody. It has also sought milestones achieved so far in the matter related to flood mitigation. EPG has filed the PIL in 2017 to flag the fragile flood management system in Kashmir and seek the court’s intervention for measures to protect Kashmir from future flood disasters. The PIL also highlights shortcomings in flood management due to which massive damage was caused during 2014 floods and seeks tangible steps to avoid such situations. EPG Convenor, Faiz Bakshi minces no words to raise red flags over illegal mining, untreated sewage discharge and condition of river embankments saying this has significant implications for the river’s ecological health, carrying capacity and flood-management system. EPG rightly states that these concerns cannot be addressed through administrative assurances alone and require transparent information, scientific assessment and effective implementation on the ground. Following incessant rains on September 7, 2014, Jhelum had crossed record 23-feet at Ram Munshi Bagh gauge, while level went over 36 feet at Sangam submerging localities on both sides of the river from south Kashmir to Srinagar. As per estimates flood water measuring about 120,000 cusecs surpassed the carrying capacity of Jhelum by five times. However no lessons have been learnt from the deluge. Despite the passage of 12 years, sustained and scientific measures are missing to increase the river’s carrying capacity. Believe it! Despite massive silt accumulation, no dredging has been undertaken in Jhelum in the last 5 years. On the other hand, unabated illegal mining in Jhelum’s tributaries —Doodh Ganga and Sukhnag has increased siltation in the river. An official report reveals that 15 lakh tonnes of riverbed material (RMB) comprising boulders, sand, nallah muck and gravel, were illegally extracted from Sukhnah river in the last several years. This wanton extraction of riverbed material severely altered the natural course of the river and extensively damaged its flora and fauna. Besides, imagine how many tons of silt must have been deposited in river Jhelum. The Ram Bagh flood spill channel looks like a forest with heavy growth of grass and other vegetation. Near Tengpora bridge, a vast chunk of the flood spill has been converted into a football ground. When water level in Jhelum rises, these bottlenecks hamper free flow of water. It is shocking to see how habitations have come up in the Jhelum’s floodplains. It was a practice of Dogra rulers to breach the Kandzal area to save Srinagar from floods. Excess water of Jhelum used to be diverted through Kandzal area and the waters would spread to Nowgam areas in central Kashmir Budgam areas. Now the Kandzal area is dotted with concrete constructions. The flood plains have been filled up! Earlier this year following incessant rains, Jhelum waters spread through its original flood plains from Shalina to Lasjan areas. The question is who allowed filling and constructions of Jhelum’s flood plains at the cost of endangering Srinagar city? Serious measures are missing to increase carrying capacity of Jhelum and restoration of its flood plains. We hope that judicial intervention will ensure long term conservation of Jhelum and restoration of its glory. And people shouldn’t forget that it’s also their responsibility to contribute their bit to protect their lifeline, the Jhelum. Author is Executive Editor, Greater Kashmir

body: Ironically the river has been fast losing both these functions in absence of conservation measures.
Jhelum originates from Verinag in south Kashmir, spans over 175 sq Kms and settles in Wular lake before flowing to Pakistan Occupied Kashmir (PoK) from Baramulla district in north Kashmir.
The river is propelled by four streams—Sundran, Brang, Arapath and Lidder is Anantnag district.
Besides small streams like Veshav and Rambiara also fed the river with fresh lease of waters.
All water bodies flow into Jhelum making it an important part of Kashmir’s interconnected hydrological system.
Despite its immense ecological importance, Jhelum is facing extreme pollution as all drains from south to north Kashmir directly flow into the river.
The irony is that instead of constructing Sewage Treatment Plants, authorities have set up hundreds of pumping stations to empty drains into the river.
The problem is compounded by dumping of solid waste and illegal sand mining.
All these factors have severely affected flora and fauna and the hydrological system of the river.
Jhelum has lost its carrying capacity also.
It has been observed that the river swells and overflows after incessant rains for even 2-3 days.

Wetlands like Hokersar, Bemina, Narakara, Batamaloo numbal, Rakh-e-arth, Anchar and Gilsar on the left and right of Jhelum, which acted as reservoirs of floodwaters, have been encroached upon, filled and converted into colonies.
Deterioration of these wetlands have affected their capacity to absorb flood water—putting extra pressure on Jhelum.
Jhelum Action Plan formulated for four towns of Anantnag, Srinagar, Sopore and Baramulla to intercept, divert, transmit sewage of these areas and treat it in STPs is still on paper.
The intervention of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir to restore the glory of Jhelum is timely.

A division bench comprising Chief Justice Dr Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Yash Paul Bourney recently sought the report after Advocate Nadeem Qadiri, assisting as amicus curiae in the Public Interest Litigation (PIL) by Environmental Policy Group on conservation of Jhelum, raised concern over deteriorating condition of Jhelum.

The Court has sought a report attesting to mining activities, proposed setting up of Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) in river Jehlum as also construction or removal of embankments for flood control of the waterbody.
It has also sought milestones achieved so far in the matter related to flood mitigation.
EPG has filed the PIL in 2017 to flag the fragile flood management system in Kashmir and seek the court’s intervention for measures to protect Kashmir from future flood disasters.
The PIL also highlights shortcomings in flood management due to which massive damage was caused during 2014 floods and seeks tangible steps to avoid such situations.

EPG Convenor, Faiz Bakshi minces no words to raise red flags over illegal mining, untreated sewage discharge and condition of river embankments saying this has significant implications for the river’s ecological health, carrying capacity and flood-management system.

EPG rightly states that these concerns cannot be addressed through administrative assurances alone and require transparent information, scientific assessment and effective implementation on the ground.

Following incessant rains on September 7, 2014, Jhelum had crossed record 23-feet at Ram Munshi Bagh gauge, while level went over 36 feet at Sangam submerging localities on both sides of the river from south Kashmir to Srinagar.
As per estimates flood water measuring about 120,000 cusecs surpassed the carrying capacity of Jhelum by five times.
However no lessons have been learnt from the deluge.
Despite the passage of 12 years, sustained and scientific measures are missing to increase the river’s carrying capacity.
Believe it!
Despite massive silt accumulation, no dredging has been undertaken in Jhelum in the last 5 years.
On the other hand, unabated illegal mining in Jhelum’s tributaries —Doodh Ganga and Sukhnag has increased siltation in the river.
An official report reveals that 15 lakh tonnes of riverbed material (RMB) comprising boulders, sand, nallah muck and gravel, were illegally extracted from Sukhnah river in the last several years.
This wanton extraction of riverbed material severely altered the natural course of the river and extensively damaged its flora and fauna.
Besides, imagine how many tons of silt must have been deposited in river Jhelum.
The Ram Bagh flood spill channel looks like a forest with heavy growth of grass and other vegetation.
Near Tengpora bridge, a vast chunk of the flood spill has been converted into a football ground.
When water level in Jhelum rises, these bottlenecks hamper free flow of water.
It is shocking to see how habitations have come up in the Jhelum’s floodplains.
It was a practice of Dogra rulers to breach the Kandzal area to save Srinagar from floods.
Excess water of Jhelum used to be diverted through Kandzal area and the waters would spread to Nowgam areas in central Kashmir Budgam areas.
Now the Kandzal area is dotted with concrete constructions.
The flood plains have been filled up!
Earlier this year following incessant rains, Jhelum waters spread through its original flood plains from Shalina to Lasjan areas.
The question is who allowed filling and constructions of Jhelum’s flood plains at the cost of endangering Srinagar city?
Serious measures are missing to increase carrying capacity of Jhelum and restoration of its flood plains.
We hope that judicial intervention will ensure long term conservation of Jhelum and restoration of its glory.
And people shouldn’t forget that it’s also their responsibility to contribute their bit to protect their lifeline, the Jhelum.
Author is Executive Editor, Greater Kashmir.
